\chapter{Eye, Mouth, Nose, and Heart}
\label{ch:bn-eye-mouth-nose-heart}
\hlchaptermodality{12}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my eye, my mouth, my nose and my heart in Bengali, and say which of those four words is settled Indo-European, which is a genuinely disputed origin, and which is borrowed whole from Sanskrit with the widest confirmed cousin family in this book.}

The chapter closes on \bn{হৃদয়}, whose root hṛd traces to PIE \'{k}érd- alongside English heart, Greek kardía and Latin cor — the widest, most secure cousin family taught anywhere in this track. The reader names all four body words (chokh, mukh, nāk, hridoy) and states each one's status: \bn{চোখ} an ardhatatsama half worn down by sound change, \bn{মুখ} a tatsama with a genuinely disputed Dravidian-versus-Indo-European origin, \bn{নাক} a tadbhava with a settled root, \bn{হৃদয়} a tatsama with a poetic tadbhava twin, \bn{হিয়া}. It reaches back to rescue Chapter 8's flapped-\bn{ড়} sound rule and its causative -\bn{আনো} grammar, neither revisited since Chapter 8.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[chokh]{\bn{চোখ} (chokh) — \textquotedblleft{}eye,\textquotedblright{} built on the root of \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:BN-C12-chokh}



\begin{quote}
A new chapter, and a new use for Chapter 3's check-in — the parts of you that check-in is actually asking about.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{চোখ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{চোখ}} — \emph{chokh} — \textbf{eye}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{চোখ}} (\emph{āmār chokh}) — my eye.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{চোখ}} is \textbf{\bn{চ}} with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{ো}} (\emph{cho}) plus \textbf{\bn{খ}} (\emph{kh}, the puffed sound you already own from \bn{খাওয়া}), silent at the end — one bare consonant, so no trailing vowel: \emph{chokh}, not \emph{chokho}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{চোখ}} traces to Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{চক্ষুস্}} (\emph{cakṣus}), \textquotedblleft{}eye\textquotedblright{} — a noun built directly on \textbf{√\bn{চক্ষ্}} (\emph{√cakṣ}, \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}), from PIE \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}e\'{k}-}, \textquotedblleft{}to appear, to see.\textquotedblright{} The nearest named cousin outside Indo-Aryan is Persian \textbf{čašm}, \textquotedblleft{}eye\textquotedblright{}; no secure English descendant is claimed for this one. And the word itself has travelled: Old Bengali softened \emph{cakṣus} down through \textbf{\bn{চখু}} (\emph{cakhu}) and \textbf{\bn{চউখ}} (\emph{coukh}) to today's \textbf{\bn{চোখ}} — half kept from Sanskrit, half worn smooth by three centuries of sound change, which is why this kind of word gets its own name, \textbf{ardhatatsama}, \textquotedblleft{}half a tatsama.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}chokh\textquotedblright{} — eye, no trailing vowel
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āmār chokh\textquotedblright{} — my eye
  \item the verb it grew from — \textquotedblleft{}cakṣ … cakṣus … chokh\textquotedblright{}
  \item the other \textquotedblleft{}see\textquotedblright{} verb you already own — \textquotedblleft{}dækhā\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give \textquotedblleft{}my eye\textquotedblright{} in Bengali. (\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{চোখ}.}) What Sanskrit verb is \bn{চোখ} built on? (\textbf{√cakṣ, \textquotedblleft{}to see.\textquotedblright{}}) Is \bn{চোখ} a tatsama, kept whole like \bn{বন্ধু}, or fully worn down like \bn{ভাই}? (\textbf{Neither — an ardhatatsama, half of each.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mukh]{\bn{মুখ} (mukh) — \textquotedblleft{}mouth, face,\textquotedblright{} a word two families both claim}

\label{lesson:BN-C12-mukh}



\begin{quote}
\bn{চোখ} (\emph{chokh}) was half old sound, half new. This word is a full tatsama again — and its own history is a real, unresolved argument among linguists.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{মুখ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{মুখ}} — \emph{mukh} — \textbf{mouth, face}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{মুখ}} (\emph{āmār mukh}) — my mouth, my face.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{মুখ}} is \textbf{\bn{ম}} with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{ু}} (\emph{mu}) plus \textbf{\bn{খ}} (\emph{kh}), silent at the end — one bare consonant again: \emph{mukh}, not \emph{mukho}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{মুখ}} is a \textbf{tatsama}, taken whole from Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{মুখ}} (\emph{mukha}) — a tadbhava twin, \textbf{\bn{মু}} (\emph{mu}), also exists, but only buried inside compound words, never standing alone. What makes \bn{মুখ} worth pausing on is where \emph{mukha} itself came from, and nobody fully agrees. One well-known account, Pokorny's, derives it from \textbf{Dravidian}, a language family with no Sanskrit or PIE connection at all. Another, Mayrhofer's, argues for an \textbf{Indo-European} source instead, pointing to the word's presence in the Rigveda and in Iranian languages as evidence it is old enough to be inherited rather than borrowed. Both scholars are serious; neither has won. The honest report is that \bn{মুখ}'s deepest root is still an open question.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mukh\textquotedblright{} — mouth, face
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āmār mukh\textquotedblright{} — my face
  \item the two rival accounts — \textquotedblleft{}Dravidian … or Indo-European\textquotedblright{}
  \item an eye, then a mouth — \textquotedblleft{}chokh … mukh\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give \textquotedblleft{}my face\textquotedblright{} in Bengali. (\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{মুখ}.}) Is \bn{মুখ}'s ultimate origin settled? (\textbf{No} — genuinely disputed between a Dravidian and an Indo-European account.) What is \bn{মুখ}'s tadbhava twin, and where does it survive? (\textbf{\bn{মু}, only inside compound words, never alone.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nāk]{\bn{নাক} (nāk) — \textquotedblleft{}nose,\textquotedblright{} the same word as English's, worn down differently}

\label{lesson:BN-C12-nak}



\begin{quote}
\bn{মুখ}'s origin was an open argument. This one is settled, and it lands somewhere you have seen before.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{নাক}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{নাক}} — \emph{nāk} — \textbf{nose}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{নাক}} (\emph{āmār nāk}) — my nose.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{নাক}} is \textbf{\bn{ন}} with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{া}} (\emph{nā}) plus \textbf{\bn{ক}} (\emph{k}), silent at the end: \emph{nāk}, not \emph{nāko}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{নাক}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{নস্}} (\emph{nas}), inherited through Prakrit \textbf{ṇakka} — a tadbhava, like \bn{ভাই} and \bn{বোন} before it. Its PIE root is \textbf{*néh\textsubscript{2}s-}, and this one is as secure as roots get: it is the direct ancestor of English \textbf{nose} itself, and of Latin \textbf{nāsus}, which gives English \textbf{nasal}. Three languages, one inherited word, three different roads of sound change — Bengali's road ran the vowel through Prakrit's \emph{a}, dropped Sanskrit's final \emph{-s}, and doubled the \emph{k} along the way.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nāk\textquotedblright{} — nose
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āmār nāk\textquotedblright{} — my nose
  \item the three cousins — \textquotedblleft{}nāk … nose … nāsus\textquotedblright{}
  \item three of this chapter's words — \textquotedblleft{}chokh … mukh … nāk\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give \textquotedblleft{}my nose\textquotedblright{} in Bengali. (\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{নাক}.}) Which two English words share \bn{নাক}'s root directly? (\textbf{Nose}, and \textbf{nasal} by way of Latin \emph{nāsus}.) Is that link as secure as \bn{মুখ}'s, or more so? (\textbf{More} — \bn{নাক}'s root is settled; \bn{মুখ}'s is still argued over.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hridoy]{\bn{হৃদয়} (hridoy) — \textquotedblleft{}heart,\textquotedblright{} the oldest cousin this book has shown you}

\label{lesson:BN-C12-hridoy}



\begin{quote}
Three body words, three different histories — half-worn, disputed, and settled. This last one closes the chapter on the most secure cousin of them all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{হৃদয়}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{হৃদয়}} — \emph{hridoy} — \textbf{heart}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{হৃদয়}} (\emph{āmār hridoy}) — my heart.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{হৃদয়}} is \textbf{\bn{হ}} with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{ৃ}} (\emph{hri}, the \textquotedblleft{}vocalic r\textquotedblright{} sign, a vowel Bengali keeps only in words borrowed from Sanskrit) plus \textbf{\bn{দ}} (\emph{dô}) plus \textbf{\bn{য়}} (\emph{yô}, a glide, not a plain stop — this is why the word ends audibly, \emph{-doy}, rather than falling silent the way \bn{দুধ} and \bn{নাক} did).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{হৃদয়}} is a \textbf{tatsama}, Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{হৃদয়}} (\emph{hṛdaya}) taken whole. A tadbhava twin also exists, \textbf{\bn{হিয়া}} (\emph{hiya}), but it lives in poetry and song rather than everyday speech — the reverse of \bn{মুখ}'s pair, where the tatsama is the everyday word. Inside \bn{হৃদয়} sits \textbf{\bn{হৃদ্}} (\emph{hṛd}), and its PIE root is \textbf{*\'{k}érd-}, \textquotedblleft{}heart\textquotedblright{} — the direct ancestor of English \textbf{heart} itself, Greek \textbf{kardía} (English \textbf{cardiac}), and Latin \textbf{cor} (English \textbf{core}, \textbf{courage}). Four languages, one root, and nowhere in this book has the family been so wide or so certain.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hridoy\textquotedblright{} — heart
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āmār hridoy\textquotedblright{} — my heart
  \item the wide family — \textquotedblleft{}hṛd … heart, kardía, cor\textquotedblright{}
  \item all four of this chapter's words — \textquotedblleft{}chokh, mukh, nāk, hridoy\textquotedblright{}
  \item one more word from Chapter 11, sharing this lesson's warmth of feeling — \textquotedblleft{}bhāi,\textquotedblright{} brother
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give \textquotedblleft{}my heart\textquotedblright{} in Bengali. (\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{হৃদয়}.}) Name three English words that share \bn{হৃদয়}'s root. (\textbf{Heart, cardiac, core} — or \textbf{courage}.) Two quick reaches further back: what does the dot under \bn{ড়} tell you to do, the letter \bn{পড়া} taught? (\textbf{Flap it}, curling the tongue back.) And what does the ending \textbf{-\bn{আনো}} do to a verb, the way \bn{ভাবা} showed on \bn{দেখা}? (\textbf{Hands the doing to someone else} — \bn{দেখা} \textquotedblleft{}see\textquotedblright{} becomes \bn{দেখানো} \textquotedblleft{}show.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
